summary:
An opinion piece arguing that career development should be treated as a component of compensation in the AI era. It opens with a thought experiment: a $120,000 role doing familiar work versus a $100,000 role offering new technology exposure, customer and decision proximity, and expanded responsibility. The author contends AI breaks the traditional link between tenure and market value, since people can spend years mastering work whose value is now declining. Helping employees improve at their current jobs is no longer enough; they need routes into higher-value work, sometimes before they are formally qualified.

An illustrative case describes a manufacturer that hired high school graduates from local car shops to paint metal components, retrained them to operate robotic arms when automation arrived, and later taught some to program the robots. Job security depended on moving up the value chain as work evolved.

The piece then argues managers, who rarely control salary, distribute development daily through assignment decisions: who attends the important meeting, who meets a customer, who presents to leadership, who takes an unfamiliar project. An example describes a warehouse employee who wanted customer contact and was nominated to a cross-functional group, which eventually led to a new role without any formal course. Another example covers a senior technology employee who asked to join a junior-level sales function to close a selling capability gap, staying two more years.

Supporting data is cited from TalentLMS and WorldatWork. The author stresses that development is personal: the same assignment can be a burden to one employee and valuable exposure to another, so managers must know what their people want to learn and where their roles no longer stretch them. Career development is positioned alongside benefits, flexibility, autonomy and job security within the total rewards or employment bargain. The text ends mid-sentence on career development as a predictor variable.

claims.claim: On-the-job experience is the leading way employees build the future skills they need, ahead of company training
claims.stat: 65% cited on-the-job experience vs 47% company training

claims.claim: Most employees say they gain new skills or knowledge by figuring things out while doing their jobs
Career growth is included alongside compensation, benefits, recognition and well-being in a total rewards framework, and career development was among the strongest predictors in the analysis
Hypothetical comparison used to frame development as pay: a familiar role versus a lower-paid but capability-building role
A senior technology employee who moved into a junior sales function to learn selling stayed with the company longer
